title: Greece: Alcmaeon, Hippocrates, Aristotle, and the Alexandrian anatomists
text:
CHAPTER 1. EARLIEST IDEAS ABOUT THE BRAIN
SECTION 1.2. GREECE: ALCMAEON, HIPPOCRATES, ARISTOTLE, AND THE ALEXANDRIAN ANATOMISTS

The brain versus the heart

Ancient Greek thinkers argued openly about where the mind lives. Two camps formed. The "encephalocentric" view held that the brain (enkephalos, "that which is in the head") is the organ of sensation and thought. The "cardiocentric" view held that the heart is. This debate lasted for centuries, and the fact that it was a debate, argued with evidence and reasoning, is itself a step forward. In this section we meet the main participants and see what kinds of evidence each side used.

Alcmaeon of Croton

Alcmaeon lived in Croton, a Greek city in southern Italy, probably in the fifth century BCE (his exact dates are uncertain). He is often associated with the Pythagorean community there, although the strength of that association is debated. Only fragments and later reports of his work survive, mostly through later writers such as Theophrastus and Aetius, so we must be careful about attributing specific claims to him.

According to these later reports, Alcmaeon held that the brain is the place where sensations are combined and where understanding arises. He is reported to have described "passages" (poroi) linking the sense organs, especially the eyes, to the brain. Some later sources say he did dissections, possibly of animal eyes, and that he noticed channels running from the eye back toward the brain, which we would identify as the optic nerves. Whether he dissected, and how much, is uncertain, and historians have argued both ways. What can be said is that he is the earliest known Greek thinker credited with placing perception and thought in the brain.

Alcmaeon is also reported to have distinguished humans from other animals by saying that humans "understand" while other animals only perceive. And he proposed a theory of health as a balance (isonomia, "equality of rights") among opposing qualities such as wet and dry, hot and cold. This balance idea became central to Greek medicine.

The Hippocratic writings

Hippocrates of Kos (roughly fifth to fourth century BCE) is the most famous name in Greek medicine. However, the large collection known as the Hippocratic Corpus was written by many authors over a long period, and it is generally not possible to say which texts, if any, Hippocrates personally wrote. When we cite "Hippocratic" ideas, we mean ideas found in this collection.

One text in the corpus is especially important for neuroscience: On the Sacred Disease. The "sacred disease" was epilepsy, which many people at the time attributed to the gods. The author of this treatise argues forcefully that epilepsy is no more sacred than any other disease, that it has a natural cause, and that the cause lies in the brain. The text contains a famous passage, which in standard English translations says that from the brain, and from the brain only, arise our pleasures, joys, laughter, and jests, as well as our sorrows, pains, griefs, and tears, and that through the brain we think, see, hear, and distinguish ugly from beautiful and good from bad. Translations differ in wording, but the claim is clear: the brain is the organ of experience and judgment, and disorders of the brain cause madness and other mental disturbances.

The physiological explanation offered in that text is not one we would accept. It involves phlegm flowing from the brain and blocking the passage of air through the vessels. But the method is important: a natural explanation is sought for a disorder of the mind, and the brain is given the central role.

Other Hippocratic texts discuss head wounds and note that injury to one side of the head may be associated with convulsions or paralysis on the opposite side of the body. This observation of contralateral effects (the left brain affecting the right side of the body and vice versa) is one of the earliest recorded clues to the crossed organization of the motor system. Exactly how consistently the Hippocratic authors stated it is something to check in the specific texts, but the general observation is attributed to them in standard histories of neurology.

The Hippocratic framework for health was the theory of the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile. Disease was imbalance. This theory dominated Western medicine until the early modern period and influenced how people thought about mood and temperament for two thousand years. Words like "melancholic" (from black bile) and "phlegmatic" are fossils of it.

Plato

Plato (about 428 to 348 BCE) was a philosopher, not a physician, but his views shaped later thinking. In the dialogue Timaeus he proposes a tripartite soul: a rational part located in the head, a spirited part in the chest, and an appetitive part below the diaphragm. So Plato placed reason in the head, which supported the encephalocentric camp, while distributing other mental functions around the body. His reasoning was largely philosophical and geometric (the head, being spherical, was suited to the divine and rational part), not anatomical.

Aristotle

Aristotle (384 to 322 BCE) was a superb biologist. He dissected many animals and wrote extensively on their anatomy, behavior, and classification. Yet on the question of the mind he chose the heart. Aristotle argued that the heart is the center of sensation and life. He observed, among other things, that the heart is located centrally, that it is warm, that it is the first organ to appear in the developing embryo he studied (he worked with chick embryos), and that blood vessels connect it to the whole body. He also noted that the brain, when touched in exposed animals, does not seem to produce sensation, and that it feels cold and wet.

What, then, was the brain for, according to Aristotle? He proposed that it was a cooling organ, which tempered the heat of the heart and the blood. In engineering terms, he thought the brain was a radiator. This sounds absurd today, but notice that it was a hypothesis based on observations: the brain is wet, it is cool to the touch compared to the heart region in a living animal, and it is richly supplied with blood. The mistake was in the interpretation, and in the weight given to some observations over others.

There is a useful lesson here for anyone who works with data. Aristotle was a careful observer, but he chose the wrong model. His evidence did not include the effects of brain injury on behavior that the Egyptian surgeon and the Hippocratic authors had noticed. When your dataset leaves out the most informative cases, a capable analyst can still reach the wrong conclusion.

The Alexandrian anatomists: Herophilus and Erasistratus

After Aristotle, the most important advances came from Alexandria in Egypt, the great city founded by Alexander the Great and ruled by the Ptolemaic dynasty. In the early third century BCE, two physicians, Herophilus of Chalcedon and Erasistratus of Ceos, carried out systematic dissections of human bodies. Ancient sources, notably the Roman writer Celsus and later the Christian writer Tertullian, also report that they performed vivisections on condemned criminals provided by the kings. Modern historians generally accept that human dissection took place in Alexandria at this time; the vivisection reports are more disputed, though some scholars take them seriously. Human dissection was otherwise rare in the ancient world, and it was largely abandoned after this period for many centuries.

None of the writings of Herophilus or Erasistratus survives directly. We know them through later authors, especially Galen. With that caveat, they are credited with several fundamental discoveries:

- Herophilus distinguished nerves from tendons and ligaments. Earlier writers often used a single word for all these cord-like structures. Herophilus is reported to have recognized that nerves arise from the brain and spinal cord.
- He is often credited with distinguishing sensory nerves from motor nerves, although the exact form of this distinction in his work is uncertain.
- He described the ventricles of the brain and identified structures that still carry names derived from his work. The "torcular Herophili," the confluence of venous sinuses at the back of the skull, is named after him. He is also credited with describing the calamus scriptorius in the floor of the fourth ventricle, so named because it resembles a reed pen.
- He described the cerebrum and the cerebellum as distinct parts.
- Erasistratus compared the convolutions of the human brain with those of other animals and is reported to have connected the greater complexity of human convolutions with greater human intelligence. This idea, while not correct in any simple form, is an early attempt to relate brain structure to cognitive ability across species.
- Erasistratus also developed a theory of "pneuma" (air or spirit) that traveled through the body. In his account, vital pneuma was carried in the arteries and "psychic" pneuma was carried in the nerves, which he thought were hollow.

The idea that nerves are hollow tubes carrying a subtle fluid or spirit would last for about two thousand years. It is wrong, but it is the first model of nerve conduction, and it is a hydraulic model. As we will see, Descartes still used a hydraulic model in the seventeenth century. Only the work on bioelectricity in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries replaced it.

How the debate stood at the end of the Hellenistic period

By the end of this period, educated physicians had good anatomical evidence that nerves come from the brain and spinal cord, that there are sensory and motor nerves, and that the brain has cavities (ventricles) and folded surfaces. Clinicians had evidence that head injuries affect movement, speech, and consciousness. Yet the authority of Aristotle meant that cardiocentric views continued among philosophers, especially among the Stoics, who placed the ruling part of the soul in the heart. The debate was not finally settled in medicine until Galen, whom we meet in the next section, made decisive experimental arguments in the second century CE.

The engineering view: three models of a control system

It may help to restate the competing views as models of a control system.

Model A, cardiocentric: the controller is in the chest. The heart receives signals and sends commands through the vessels. The brain is a heat exchanger. Prediction: damage to the brain should affect temperature regulation but not sensation or movement.

Model B, encephalocentric with hydraulic signaling: the controller is in the head. Signals travel through hollow nerves carried by pneuma. Prediction: damage to the brain or cutting a nerve should abolish sensation or movement in the region served by that nerve.

Model C, distributed: different mental functions are located in different organs, as in Plato's tripartite soul.

The data on head injuries and nerve injuries favor model B, and that is the direction medicine moved. It is a good habit to state your models in a way that makes predictions that can be tested by intervention. That habit was not yet fully developed in the ancient world, but Galen came closer than anyone.

Bridge to AI: where is the "intelligence"?

The brain versus heart debate has a modern echo. When we talk about an AI system, where is the intelligence? Is it in the model weights, in the training data, in the prompt, or in the larger system that includes tools, memory, and human feedback? Engineers who build robots face a related question: how much of a robot's competence comes from the controller, and how much from the body and its mechanics (for example, a passive dynamic walker that walks downhill with no controller at all)? This view, sometimes called embodied or morphological computation, reminds us that the brain is not a disembodied computer. It is a controller tightly coupled to a body, much as Aristotle insisted the heart and body were tightly coupled. The ancient debate was wrong on the facts, but the question of where computation happens in a system is still a good one.

Another echo concerns the idea that brain complexity, measured by folding, tracks intelligence. In AI, it has often been observed that larger models with more parameters, trained on more data, tend to perform better, a pattern described by empirical scaling laws. But neither in brains nor in machines is size the only factor. Architecture, training, and the match between the system and its tasks all matter. Erasistratus's intuition that structure relates to capability was a good start; the details turned out to be much more complicated.

Summary

- Alcmaeon of Croton is the earliest Greek thinker reported to have placed perception and understanding in the brain.
- The Hippocratic text On the Sacred Disease argued that epilepsy has a natural cause in the brain and that the brain is the organ of thought and emotion.
- Plato located reason in the head; Aristotle, a careful biologist, located sensation in the heart and saw the brain as a cooling organ.
- In Alexandria, Herophilus and Erasistratus dissected human bodies, distinguished nerves from tendons, described the ventricles and the cerebellum, and treated nerves as hollow channels for pneuma.
- The hydraulic model of nerve function would dominate until the discovery of bioelectricity.
